items.question_text: A 58-year-old woman attends a Melbourne general practice on a Thursday afternoon for a repeat of transdermal oestradiol, which she has used since a surgical menopause at 49. She works as a school registrar, walks to the station each day, and has no chest pain, breast lump, nipple discharge, skin dimpling, or axillary swelling. Her mother is alive at 84 and has never had cancer. An aunt had breast cancer at 71 and is also alive. She took the oral contraceptive pill for less than a year in her twenties, had two children before 30, and breastfed both. She drinks a glass of wine on weekends and has never smoked. Her last BreastScreen report, 26 months ago, was normal and described heterogeneously dense tissue. She has spent the week reading online forums in which women with dense breasts were told that mammography is almost useless and that they should pay for a private contrast MRI every year. A private radiologist who imaged her shoulder last year made a similar offhand comment about density. She is worried that density means the mammogram missed something, and she asks whether she should abandon the program and book a private contrast MRI instead. Her BMI is 27. Examination of both breasts and axillae is normal. There is no skin change and no nipple retraction. She takes no other medicines and has no implants. A recent full blood count, done for fatigue that resolved, was normal. She is not on an anticoagulant. Her blood pressure today is 128/76. She is not diabetic. A cholesterol check last month was acceptable. She can attend a screening centre within two weeks. Her GP notes that she is squarely inside the invited age band and that her family history does not meet criteria for a familial cancer clinic. She has capacity, is not pregnant, and asks, plainly, what she should actually do this year. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Book the next BreastScreen mammogram now
Arrange annual breast MRI as her population screening test
Replace mammography with screening ultrasound because the last report mentioned density
Defer all imaging until 65 because the last mammogram was normal
Measure CA 15-3 today and screen only if it is raised
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Book the next BreastScreen mammogram now

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
A symptom-free 58-year-old who is 26 months past a normal mammogram is due for BreastScreen mammography, not MRI or ultrasound prompted by density or an aunt's cancer.

2. THE RULE
BreastScreen invitation and who may attend

3. WHY THIS OPTION
A matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
She is symptom-free, 58, and 26 months past a normal mammogram, so she is due for the BreastScreen test. Heterogeneous density and an aunt diagnosed at 71 do not move her onto MRI. Hormone therapy is not a reason to change the program test.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Book the next BreastScreen mammogram now

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Invite a symptom-free woman aged 50–74 to BreastScreen every 2 years.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
BreastScreen invites women aged 50–74 for mammography every 2 years.

---

items.question_text: A 46-year-old woman in Adelaide has asked the receptionist for a BreastScreen referral after a friend said free mammograms do not start until 50 and that asking earlier is a waste of everyone's time. She has no lump, pain, nipple change, or skin thickening. Her sister had a fibroadenoma excised at 29. There is no relative with breast or ovarian cancer. She is otherwise well, has never had breast imaging, had one child at 32, and breastfed for four months. She works in a call centre, does not smoke, and drinks rarely. She is anxious because a colleague was diagnosed at 48, and she has convinced herself that waiting until 50 is reckless. On examination both breasts are normal, with no axillary nodes. She is not pregnant. She asks whether booking now is pointless, whether she will be turned away, and whether she should instead pay for a private ultrasound to be safe. A local radiology group has already quoted her $480 for a bilateral ultrasound and mammogram. Her GP records show no breast complaint in six years at the practice. There is no chest-wall radiation in her history. A cousin had a benign cyst drained at 40. She has private health insurance and wants a clear answer on whether the public system will accept her at 46. Blood pressure is 122/74. She takes no regular medicines. A recent cervical screen was normal. She can attend a centre next week if advised. Examination today adds nothing. What is the most appropriate advice about BreastScreen?  She has never used hormone therapy. Her periods stopped at 44. There is no personal history of atypical hyperplasia or lobular carcinoma in situ. A maternal grandmother died of unrelated heart disease at 80. She is up to date with cervical screening. The receptionist has already told her the referral will be rejected, which is why she is asking the GP directly. She is prepared to pay privately if the public pathway is closed to her, but she would prefer not to. The examination adds no mass, no skin change, and no node. The decision is whether a 46-year-old asymptomatic woman can attend BreastScreen now.
options: Tell her she is ineligible for a free mammogram until she turns 50
She can book a BreastScreen mammogram now, but she will not be routinely invited until 50
Start annual mammography from today until 74 because she has asked early
Screen with ultrasound every year until she enters the invitation group
A normal examination today replaces imaging until 50
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. She can book a BreastScreen mammogram now, but she will not be routinely invited until 50

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
At 46 she can book BreastScreen but is not in the routine invitation group, and a fibroadenoma in a sister does not create an annual pathway.

2. THE RULE
BreastScreen invitation and who may attend

3. WHY THIS OPTION
B matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Invitation and access are different. BreastScreen invites women aged 50–74. From 40 she may still book a free mammogram every 2 years. A sister's fibroadenoma is not a familial-cancer indication, so she does not need annual imaging.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
She can book a BreastScreen mammogram now, but she will not be routinely invited until 50

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Women aged 40–49 may book BreastScreen but are not the invited cohort.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
Invitation age is 50–74. Attendance is open from 40.

---

items.question_text: A 61-year-old woman in Brisbane notices a new hard lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast while showering. It has been there for three weeks. She had a normal BreastScreen mammogram 14 months ago. There is no nipple discharge. She is a non-smoker, takes perindopril for hypertension, and has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On examination there is a 2 cm firm, irregular mass, tethered to skin, with a palpable left axillary node. She is frightened and asks whether she should simply wait for her next BreastScreen invitation, which she believes is the proper pathway, or book the routine screening mammogram a few months early. Her sister has told her that screening clinics are faster than hospital clinics. She has no fever, no recent trauma, and no signs of infection. The remainder of the examination is normal. She is systemically well, weight stable, and has no bone pain. A BreastScreen letter from 14 months ago is in her bag and is normal. The axillary node is firm and about 1.5 cm. She is post-menopausal on no hormone therapy. Her sister has offered to drive her to a BreastScreen van in the suburb next week. The GP can feel the mass and the node. Bloods last month were unremarkable. She is not anticoagulated. What is the most appropriate next step?  She noticed the lump on a Saturday and has checked it daily since. It has not changed with her cycle because she no longer has cycles. There is no nipple inversion of long standing. A previous cyst was aspirated on the other side ten years ago and did not recur. She is a non-drinker. Her last mammogram report, which she has brought, says no significant abnormality and BIRADS 1. The node in the axilla was not present at her last GP visit six months ago for a flu vaccine. She is afebrile. There is no erythema. Weight is stable at 68 kg. The question is whether a new mass with a node goes to screening or to diagnostic assessment.
options: Use the BreastScreen appointment and review her once the screening report returns
Reassure her that a mobile lump under 45 can be reviewed in 6 months
Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram
Start tamoxifen now and image only if the lump is still there in 3 months
Request CA 15-3 and a chest X-ray as the first screen
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
A 3-week hard breast lump needs diagnostic triple assessment. A convenient BreastScreen slot does not convert it into a screening episode.

2. THE RULE
Breast symptom or high risk is not routine BreastScreen

3. WHY THIS OPTION
C matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
A new hard lump is a symptom. BreastScreen is for women without breast symptoms, and a screening slot does not investigate a palpable mass. She needs diagnostic triple assessment: clinical review, diagnostic imaging, and needle biopsy as indicated.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
A new breast lump is a diagnostic referral, not a BreastScreen appointment.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
Symptoms leave BreastScreen.

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

items.question_text: A 77-year-old woman in Hobart has not been invited to BreastScreen for two years. She is well, has no breast symptom, and had normal screens throughout her sixties. Her daughter has read that screening stops at 74 and has told her she is no longer allowed to attend. She is a retired teacher, lives alone, drives, and has no cognitive impairment. There is no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. She takes a statin and vitamin D. Examination is normal. She asks whether the program has closed to her permanently, whether attending would be against the rules, and whether she should instead pay for a private mammogram every year for the rest of her life. She is not frail, has a life expectancy well beyond a few years, and can consent for herself. Her GP is aware that invitation and access are not the same thing at this age.  She has attended BreastScreen regularly since 52 and has every normal report in a folder at home. Her daughter read a news article saying the program ends at 74 and has booked her a private annual mammogram at $320 a time. She is a retired teacher, lives alone, drives, and manages her own medicines. There is no cognitive impairment. She takes atorvastatin and vitamin D only. There is no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Examination today is normal, with no mass and no node. She is not frail. Her GP estimates her life expectancy is well beyond five years. She asks whether the program has closed to her permanently, whether attending would be against the rules, and whether private imaging every year is now her only option. She can consent for herself. The question is invitation versus access after 74. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Further mammography is contraindicated once she is over 74
She must continue annual mammography until 80 to stay enrolled
Transfer her to annual screening MRI because invitation has stopped
She is no longer invited, but she may choose to book BreastScreen after a discussion of benefit
Replace mammography with 2-yearly clinical examination only
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. She is no longer invited, but she may choose to book BreastScreen after a discussion of benefit

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
After 74 she is no longer invited, but mammography is not forbidden. She can still choose BreastScreen.

2. THE RULE
BreastScreen invitation and who may attend

3. WHY THIS OPTION
D matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Active invitation stops after 74. That is not a ban. A well 76-year-old with no breast symptoms may choose to keep attending after a discussion of benefit, overdiagnosis, and competing health problems. Her last screen was 18 months ago, so she is not even due today.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
She is no longer invited, but she may choose to book BreastScreen after a discussion of benefit

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Women aged 75 and over are not invited, but may choose to attend BreastScreen.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
End of invitation is not a contraindication.

---

items.question_text: A 42-year-old woman is found to carry a pathogenic BRCA1 variant after her sister died of ovarian cancer at 46. She has no breast symptom. She has been told by a relative to just join BreastScreen early and have an ordinary mammogram every two years like everyone else. She has two children, breastfed both, does not smoke, and has not had risk-reducing surgery. She is anxious, has been reading conflicting advice online, and asks whether the national screening program is enough now that the gene result is known. Examination of breasts and axillae is normal. She is not pregnant. There is no lump. Her GP has the genetic report. A colleague suggests that because she is under 50 she cannot access any imaging at all, and another suggests a single private ultrasound and discharge.  The BRCA1 result arrived last week from a familial cancer service that tested her after her sister's death. She has no breast symptom, no ovarian symptom, and has not had risk-reducing surgery. She has two children, breastfed both, and does not smoke. A relative has told her to join BreastScreen early and have an ordinary mammogram every two years. She has been reading conflicting advice online, some of it about MRI and some about ultrasound. Examination of breasts and axillae is normal. She is not pregnant. There is no lump. Her GP has the genetic report in the file. A colleague has suggested she is too young for any imaging, and another has suggested a single private ultrasound and discharge. She is anxious and wants to know if the national program is enough now that the gene is known. The pathway is not routine screening. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Routine BreastScreen from age 50 is sufficient for a BRCA1 carrier
Population ultrasound from age 30 can replace specialist review during pregnancy
Bilateral mastectomy must be booked before any further imaging or pregnancy care
Defer every breast decision until she has finished childbearing
Refer to a familial cancer service for an intensified surveillance plan
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Refer to a familial cancer service for an intensified surveillance plan

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
BRCA1 is not covered by waiting for BreastScreen at 50. She should be referred to a familial cancer service, not booked for immediate mastectomy.

2. THE RULE
Breast symptom or high risk is not routine BreastScreen

3. WHY THIS OPTION
E matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
A pathogenic BRCA1 variant is not average risk, and pregnancy does not park that fact until BreastScreen invitation at 50. She needs a familial cancer service to plan surveillance, usually earlier and with MRI considered. Surgery may be discussed later. It is not an emergency order before antenatal care.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Refer to a familial cancer service for an intensified surveillance plan

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
A known high-risk mutation needs a familial pathway, not routine BreastScreen alone.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
Population invitation ages assume average risk.

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

items.question_text: A 55-year-old man asks whether he should enrol in BreastScreen because his mother had breast cancer at 78. He has no breast lump, nipple discharge, or skin change. He is well, takes no medicines, and has never had breast imaging. There is no other family history. He works as a driver and is a non-smoker. Examination shows no mass and no axillary node. He has read that men can get breast cancer and assumes there must be a population mammography program for asymptomatic men, parallel to the women's program. He asks for the invitation letter and the two-yearly recall. His GP notes he is asymptomatic and has no personal high-risk feature.  He is 55, well, and takes no medicines. His mother had breast cancer at 78 and is alive. He has no breast lump, no nipple discharge, and no skin change. There is no other family history of breast or ovarian cancer. He works as a driver and has never smoked. Examination shows no mass and no axillary node. He has read that men can get breast cancer and assumes there is a population mammography program for asymptomatic men, with invitation letters and two-yearly recall, parallel to the women's program. He has asked the receptionist for the enrolment form. He is asymptomatic and has no personal high-risk feature such as prior chest radiation or a known pathogenic variant. The question is whether an asymptomatic man is offered population breast screening. What is the most appropriate advice?  He has no gynaecomastia and no medication that would raise his own risk. A chest X-ray last year for a visa was normal. He is asking for enrolment in a population program, not for investigation of a symptom. Population breast screening is not offered to an asymptomatic man.
options: Population breast screening is not offered to an asymptomatic man
Enrol him for 2-yearly mammography if he is willing to pay
Annual screening ultrasound until 74 is the male equivalent
Check CA 15-3 every 2 years alongside his lipid tests
Start tamoxifen for 5 years as the male prevention program
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Population breast screening is not offered to an asymptomatic man

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
An asymptomatic man is not enrolled in BreastScreen, including if he offers to pay.

2. THE RULE
BreastScreen invitation and who may attend

3. WHY THIS OPTION
A matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
BreastScreen is a population program for women. Willingness to pay does not create a male invitation cohort. He has no lump, so this is not a diagnostic referral either.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Population breast screening is not offered to an asymptomatic man

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
There is no population mammography program for asymptomatic men.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
BreastScreen does not have a male population arm.

---

items.question_text: A 47-year-old man in Perth asks for a bowel cancer screening kit. A friend told him the government posts them from 40. He has no rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, weight loss, or anaemia. His father had a polyp removed at 72. He is otherwise well, BMI 29, non-smoker. He has never had a colonoscopy. He is keen to get on the list and is irritated that nothing has arrived in the post. Examination is unremarkable and there is no abdominal mass. He asks whether requesting a kit now is allowed, or whether he must wait until the automatic mail-out.  He is 47, BMI 29, and a non-smoker. He has no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, no weight loss, and no anaemia on a blood count done last month for an insurance medical. His father had a polyp removed at 72. He has never had a colonoscopy. A friend told him kits are posted from age 40, and he is irritated that nothing has arrived. Examination shows no abdominal mass. He asks whether he can request a free kit now or must wait for the automatic mail-out at 50. He is otherwise well and can complete a kit at home this week if one is available. The question is request versus automatic invitation. What is the most appropriate next step?  He works in construction and has private insurance but would prefer the free kit. There is no family history of colorectal cancer under 60. A faecal occult blood test was never done. He is not on aspirin or an anticoagulant. Weight is stable. He can follow instructions for the kit if one is issued. The friend who mentioned age 40 was mistaken about the mail-out. Requesting a kit at 47 is allowed. Automatic mailing starts at 50.
options: He is ineligible until his 50th birthday, so do not request a kit
He can request a free kit now, and automatic mailing starts at 50
A kit should already have been mailed automatically at 45
Book colonoscopy as the first program test because his wife was invited
The kit is only for people who have already noticed bleeding
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. He can request a free kit now, and automatic mailing starts at 50

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
At 47 he requests a bowel kit. The mailed kit his wife received is the 50–74 path, not proof he was missed.

2. THE RULE
Bowel screening age, mail-out and who completes a kit

3. WHY THIS OPTION
B matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Since 1 July 2024 the program age is 45–74. At 47 he requests the first kit. His wife's mailed kit reflects the 50–74 path, not a missed invitation. He has no symptoms, so colonoscopy is not the entry test.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
He can request a free kit now, and automatic mailing starts at 50

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Ages 45–49 request a bowel kit. Automatic mail starts at 50.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
45–49 request the first kit. 50–74 are mailed one.

---

items.question_text: A 62-year-old woman receives her National Bowel Cancer Screening kit in the mail. She has no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, and no weight loss. She had a normal colonoscopy eight years ago for a positive kit at the time. She is well, takes a statin, and is unsure whether she still needs to complete this kit or whether the old colonoscopy covers her for life. She asks if she can ignore the mail-out. There is no family history of colorectal cancer. Examination is normal.  She is 62 and has just received her National Bowel Cancer Screening kit. She has no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, and no weight loss. She had a normal colonoscopy eight years ago after a previous positive kit. She takes a statin and is otherwise well. There is no family history of colorectal cancer. She believes the old colonoscopy covers her for life and asks if she can ignore the mail-out. Examination is normal. Haemoglobin last year was normal. She is inside the mailed age band and has no symptom that would replace the kit with a diagnostic test. The question is whether she completes this kit. What is the most appropriate next step?  She is a retired nurse and remembers the old colonoscopy clearly. The report, which she has, showed diverticula only. She has had no polyps. She is not iron deficient. She asks if the program writes to people who ignore a kit. She is happy to do the test if it is still required. The eight-year gap means the old colonoscopy does not replace this kit. She should complete and return it.
options: Discard the kit and book a screening colonoscopy because she is over 60
Keep the kit until she next sees blood, then post it
Complete and return the kit
Do the kit only if a fresh full blood count shows anaemia
Cancel it and request a CEA with her annual lipids
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Complete and return the kit

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
An asymptomatic 63-year-old who receives a kit should complete it. A friend's colonoscopy and old haemorrhoids do not replace the kit.

2. THE RULE
Bowel screening age, mail-out and who completes a kit

3. WHY THIS OPTION
C matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
She is in the mailed cohort and has no current bowel symptoms. Old treated haemorrhoids do not upgrade her to primary colonoscopy. The program test is the immunochemical kit.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Complete and return the kit

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Ages 50–74 complete the mailed immunochemical kit if they have no bowel symptoms.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
The mailed test is the immunochemical kit every 2 years.

items.question_text: A 66-year-old man completes a mailed immunochemical kit. The result is positive. He feels well, has no bleeding, and a friend tells him to repeat the kit in case it was a false alarm, and to avoid colonoscopy. He had no recent colonoscopy. He asks his GP to order a second kit and keep it in the community. Haemoglobin is normal.  He is 66 and has completed a mailed immunochemical kit. The result is positive. He feels well and has no bleeding. A friend has told him to repeat the kit in case it was a false alarm and to avoid colonoscopy. He had no colonoscopy in the last two years. Haemoglobin is normal. He asks his GP to order a second kit and keep the problem in the community. He is anxious about the procedure but can attend a public list. The positive kit is the reason for the visit. The next step is not another kit. What is the most appropriate next step?  He has never had a colonoscopy. His brother had a polyp at 68. He is not anaemic. He has read that immunochemical tests have false positives and wants laboratory proof before a procedure. A second kit is not the pathway after a positive program result. Colonoscopy is the next test. Delaying for a repeat kit risks losing him to follow-up.  He works shifts and is worried about time off for a colonoscopy. A normal haemoglobin does not clear a positive kit. Repeating the kit is the common error. Referral for colonoscopy is the pathway.
options: Repeat the kit in 6 weeks after a period of dietary restriction
File the result and send the next kit in 2 years
Order CEA and review the result in 6 months if it is normal
Refer him for colonoscopy
Start oral iron and repeat the kit only if the haemoglobin falls
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Refer him for colonoscopy

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
A positive program kit goes to colonoscopy. Repeating it after steak is the retired guaiac move, not the current pathway.

2. THE RULE
Positive kit or symptoms or recent colonoscopy is not another kit

3. WHY THIS OPTION
D matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
A positive immunochemical kit is not confirmed by repeating it after a diet change. Diet was a guaiac-era worry. He needs colonoscopy. A normal haemoglobin does not retire a positive screen.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Refer him for colonoscopy

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
A positive program kit needs colonoscopy, not a repeat kit.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR

She also has a mailed bowel kit at home, unopened, and asks whether she should just do the kit rather than make a fuss. She has no weight loss. Examination of the abdomen is normal. Rectal examination shows no mass. A colleague says the kit is the national pathway and should come first.  She is 58 and has had bright red rectal bleeding on the paper for six weeks. She also has a mailed bowel kit at home, unopened, and asks whether she should just do the kit rather than make a fuss. She has no weight loss. Abdominal examination is normal. Rectal examination shows no mass. A colleague has said the kit is the national pathway and should come first. She is systemically well. The bleeding is a symptom. The kit is a screening tool for people without symptoms. The next step is diagnostic, not a kit. What is the most appropriate next step? Abdominal and rectal examination show no mass. The unopened kit is a screening kit for asymptomatic people. Symptoms take her out of that pathway. She needs a diagnostic colonoscopy, not a kit result.  She has private insurance and could have a colonoscopy within a fortnight. The kit at home is irrelevant once bleeding is present. Diagnostic colonoscopy is the next step.

Wait 6 weeks for the bleeding to settle, then post a kit
Order CEA today and book colonoscopy only if it is raised
Reassure him that bright bleeding at 60 is haemorrhoids until a kit says otherwise
Refer for diagnostic colonoscopy rather than using the screening kit

She became sexually active a year ago, has had one partner, and completed the school HPV vaccine course. There is no abnormal bleeding, no pelvic pain, and no immune suppression. She is not pregnant. The practice nurse has already said a test is not due, and she has come to the GP for a second opinion. Her mother is insistent that delaying is unsafe. Routine cervical screening in Australia starts at 25, not at the old Pap age. A test today would follow an outdated schedule. She does not need screening now. C matches the rule on the facts given.

The program invites people with a cervix from 25 to 74, every 5 years, once they have had sexual contact. She is 22 and has not had sexual contact, so a routine test is not due. Her mother's start age belongs to the retired Pap program. School vaccination does not pull the start age forward.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

Routine screening is not due at 22

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Routine cervical screening starts at 25, not at the old Pap age of 18.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR

items.question_text: A 59-year-old man who still smokes, with a 40 pack-year history, attends after coughing up about a tablespoon of blood on two mornings this week. He has no fever and no chest pain. He has seen the lung screening advertisements and asks for a low-dose CT like the ads, rather than a diagnostic clinic appointment. He has no previous chest imaging. Haemoptysis is a symptom. It is investigated as a possible cancer, not screened. Enrolment in the screening program is the wrong pathway for someone who is bleeding. He needs assessment of the haemoptysis. What is the most appropriate next step?  The blood is fresh and has happened on two separate mornings. He is a current heavy smoker. There is no infective prodrome. Screening programs are for people without symptoms of the target cancer. Haemoptysis is such a symptom. He needs a diagnostic pathway, not an invitation into a screening round. A low-dose screening CT is the wrong request.  He is haemodynamically stable. That does not make the bleeding a screening issue. Diagnostic assessment comes first.
options: Complete the screening request for a low-dose CT
Arrange a chest X-ray in 6 months and then decide about screening
Investigate the haemoptysis rather than enrol him in screening
Ask him to quit for 4 weeks and then sign the screening form
Send sputum cytology as the program entry test
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Investigate the haemoptysis rather than enrol him in screening

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
Haemoptysis takes him out of the lung screening program and into diagnostic assessment, even though his pack-years would otherwise qualify.

2. THE RULE
Lung screening test, pack-years, quit time and symptoms

3. WHY THIS OPTION
C matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Haemoptysis is a symptom suggestive of lung cancer. The program is for people without those symptoms. A free low-dose CT form is the wrong request. He needs diagnostic assessment. Quitting does not come before that.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Investigate the haemoptysis rather than enrol him in screening

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Haemoptysis is investigated. It is not a screening low-dose CT.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
The program requires no symptoms suggestive of lung cancer.

items.question_text: A 55-year-old man asks for lung cancer screening because he is over 50 and once smoked. He smoked socially, a few cigarettes at weekends, for about five years in his twenties, and quit at 30. The total is well under 30 pack-years. He is asymptomatic, with no cough, no haemoptysis, and no weight loss. A friend of a similar age has been accepted into the program after a 40-year heavy smoking history, and he assumes age plus any smoking is enough. The program requires a 30 pack-year threshold. He does not meet it. A chest X-ray is not the alternative screening test. What is the most appropriate advice?  The smoking history is light and remote. Five social years do not reach 30 pack-years. He quit 25 years ago. He has no symptom. Age over 50 is necessary but not sufficient. He does not meet the pack-year threshold to enter. Offering him a chest X-ray instead would also be wrong. The advice is that he is not eligible.  No symptom, no threshold pack-years, quit long ago. He is not eligible. Age alone does not enrol him.
options: She is eligible on age and current smoking
Offer annual chest X-ray because she is under 30 pack-years
She must wait until 55 even if the pack-years later qualify
She does not meet the pack-year threshold to enter
She can self-request a screening PET scan
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. She does not meet the pack-year threshold to enter

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
Ten cigarettes a day for 20 years is 10 pack-years, below the 30 required to enter lung screening.

2. THE RULE
Lung screening test, pack-years, quit time and symptoms

3. WHY THIS OPTION
D matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Ten cigarettes a day for 20 years is 10 pack-years. Entry needs at least 30, plus age 50–70 and current smoking or quit within 10 years, without symptoms. The poster omitted the pack-year line. A chest X-ray or PET is not the alternative program.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
She does not meet the pack-year threshold to enter

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Lung screening needs 30 pack-years, not age and any smoking history.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
Pack-years are packs per day times years.

---

items.question_text: A 54-year-old man with no urinary symptoms attends asking to join the national PSA screening program. He has read about BreastScreen and the bowel kit program and assumes there is an equivalent national program for prostate cancer, with invitation letters and a fixed recall interval. There is no family history of prostate cancer. Examination is normal. He is not on a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor. He is asymptomatic. There is no national PSA screening program to enrol him in. Opportunistic discussion of the PSA test is a different conversation from enrolment in a program. The answer to the question he has asked is that no such program exists. What is the most appropriate advice?  He is average risk and asymptomatic. There is no national invitation program for PSA. BreastScreen and the bowel kit program are organised screening. PSA is not. He cannot enrol. A discussion about the limits of the PSA test can happen if he asks about the test itself. That is not the same as joining a program. The answer to enrolment is no.  He leaves with a clear answer on enrolment. There is no program. Any later talk about PSA is separate.
options: He will be mailed a PSA kit every 2 years, like the bowel program
Annual PSA is required for men from 50 to 74
A prostate MRI every 2 years is the population screening test
A normal PSA today would end any later discussion of prostate tests
There is no national PSA screening program to enrol him in
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. There is no national PSA screening program to enrol him in

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
There is no national PSA program to enrol him in. A request can lead to a shared decision, not a mail-out.

2. THE RULE
No national PSA, melanoma or average-risk ovarian screening

3. WHY THIS OPTION
E matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Australia does not run a population PSA program and does not mail PSA kits. A man who asks can have a shared discussion of benefit and harm. That discussion is not enrolment, and MRI is not a population screen.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
There is no national PSA screening program to enrol him in

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
There is no national PSA screening program.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
Do not describe PSA as a mailed national program.

---

items.question_text: A 49-year-old woman with many moles asks to enrol in the national melanoma screening program. None of the moles is changing, itching, or bleeding. She has no personal history of melanoma and no first-degree relative with melanoma. She expects invitation letters in the way BreastScreen works. There is no national skin-cancer screening program. A clinical skin check may be offered as part of a consultation if there is a reason. It is not an enrolled population screen with a mail-out. She cannot join a program that does not exist. What is the most appropriate advice?  No mole is new or changing. There is no ulcerated lesion. She has no family history of melanoma. There is no national melanoma screening program with invitations. She cannot enrol. A skin check in a consultation is a clinical service, not a population program. The request to join a program has no program to join.  No changing lesion, no program. She cannot enrol. A clinical review of a specific mole would be a different visit.
options: There is no national skin-cancer screening program to enrol her in
Complete the national recall so she is photographed every 2 years
The program is annual biopsy of two moles, whether or not they change
A normal skin check at 45 ends any later skin surveillance
She should have a screening PET scan as the entry test

National programs cover bowel, breast, cervix, and lung. There is no population melanoma program with a government recall. A clinic package is a private service, not program enrolment. A changing lesion would be diagnostic, and she has none.

items.question_text: A 51-year-old woman at average risk asks for a yearly CA 125 blood test and a pelvic ultrasound to screen for ovarian cancer. She has no pelvic pain, no bloating, no urinary change, and no postmenopausal bleeding. There is no significant family history of ovarian, breast, or related cancers. A friend has these tests yearly and has told her this is standard screening, like a mammogram. Population ovarian screening with CA 125 and ultrasound is not recommended for average-risk women. The tests are not a national program. Ordering them every year would be an unproven add-on, not screening. What is the most appropriate advice?  She is average risk. No symptom. No significant family history. CA 125 and pelvic ultrasound have been tested as a screening pair and are not recommended for population screening in this group. A friend having the tests does not create a program. Ordering them yearly would not be appropriate screening. The advice is not to start that pair as a screen.  No symptom and average risk. The pair of tests is not recommended as a screen. She should not start yearly CA 125 and ultrasound for this purpose.
options: Enrol her in annual CA 125 and pelvic ultrasound
Population ovarian screening is not recommended on this history
CA 125 every 6 months can replace the ultrasound
A single normal CA 125 today ends her familial risk
Start a combined oral contraceptive as the screening test
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Population ovarian screening is not recommended on this history

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
Annual CA 125 and ultrasound are not a screening program for an asymptomatic woman whose only affected relative was diagnosed at 72.

2. THE RULE
No national PSA, melanoma or average-risk ovarian screening

3. WHY THIS OPTION
B matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
There is no effective population screen for ovarian cancer, and CA 125 plus ultrasound is not a national program. One relative diagnosed at 72 does not by itself open a high-risk mutation pathway. The oral contraceptive pill is not a screening test.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Population ovarian screening is not recommended on this history

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Average-risk women are not offered CA 125 or ultrasound to screen for ovarian cancer.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR

items.question_text: A 49-year-old woman requests her first bowel cancer screening kit. She is asymptomatic, with no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, and no weight loss. She believes she is already in the automatic mail-out group because she is nearly 50 and has heard that kits arrive from 50. Automatic mailing starts at 50. At 49 she is not yet in the mailed cohort. She can request a free kit now. Waiting for a letter that will not come yet is the error. There is no family history that would move her to colonoscopy instead. Examination is normal. What is the most appropriate advice?  She is 49 and well. Automatic kits are mailed from 50. She is one year early for the mail-out. She can request a kit. There is no symptom and no family history that would replace a kit with colonoscopy. Waiting for a letter is unnecessary. The correct step is to request the kit.  No symptom, age 49, can request a kit. The mail-out has not started for her. Requesting is the step.
options: A kit will be mailed automatically within the year, so she should wait for it
She cannot screen until 50, so a request now will be rejected
She needs to request the first kit rather than wait for a mail-out
Colonoscopy is the first program test at 49
She should wait until she has a symptom before requesting a kit
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. She needs to request the first kit rather than wait for a mail-out

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
At 49 the first bowel kit is requested. It is not mailed automatically, and she does not wait until 50.

2. THE RULE
Bowel screening age, mail-out and who completes a kit

3. WHY THIS OPTION
C matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
At 49 she is in the 45–49 band. The first kit is requested. Automatic mailing is what her neighbour received at 51. Once she completes a kit, later kits are mailed every 2 years. Symptoms would be a reason not to use the kit.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
She needs to request the first kit rather than wait for a mail-out

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES

10. MEMORY ANCHOR

items.question_text: A 46-year-old woman finds a firm lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. It has been there for three weeks. She is otherwise well, has no family history of breast cancer, and has never had a mammogram. She asks to be enrolled in BreastScreen so the lump can be checked on the program. A receptionist has told her the next screening round is in six months and she should wait. BreastScreen is a screening program for women without symptoms. A new lump is a diagnostic problem, not a screening invitation. She needs clinical assessment and diagnostic imaging, not a place on a screening list. What is the most appropriate advice? The lump is new, unilateral, and persistent. Waiting for a screening round delays assessment of a symptomatic breast. Screening mammography is not the pathway for a woman who has already found a lump. She should be referred for diagnostic assessment now, not booked into the next invitation cycle. Nothing about her age or the absence of a family history converts a symptomatic breast into a screening case. The program is for women who have no breast symptom. She has one. That single fact changes the pathway.
options: Enrol her in BreastScreen and wait for the next round
Reassure her that a firm lump at 46 is benign and review in a year
Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram
Arrange a screening mammogram only, with no clinical examination
Start tamoxifen while waiting for the screening appointment
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
A symptom-free 58-year-old who is 26 months past a normal mammogram is due for BreastScreen mammography, not MRI or ultrasound prompted by density or an aunt's cancer.

2. THE RULE
Breast symptom or high risk is not routine BreastScreen

3. WHY THIS OPTION
C matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
A woman with a breast symptom is not a screening candidate. BreastScreen is for asymptomatic women in the eligible age range. A new lump needs diagnostic assessment, not a screening invitation. Waiting for the next round, or arranging only a screening mammogram, delays proper assessment.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Invite a symptom-free woman aged 50–74 to BreastScreen every 2 years.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
BreastScreen invites women aged 50–74 for mammography every 2 years.

items.question_text: A 58-year-old man completed a National Bowel Cancer Screening kit. The result is positive. He feels well, has no rectal bleeding, and his weight is stable. He asks for another kit to check the result, because he has read that the test can be wrong and he would prefer to avoid a colonoscopy. A colleague says a second kit is reasonable if he is anxious. A positive screening kit is not confirmed by repeating the same test. A second kit can be negative and falsely reassure him. The next step after a positive kit is colonoscopy. What is the most appropriate advice? He is in the screening age range and the kit was done correctly. Feeling well does not clear a positive result. The kit is a screening test, not a diagnosis, and it is not a test that is repeated to confirm itself. Colonoscopy is the diagnostic step. Offering another kit delays that and can miss a cancer the first test found. Anxiety is managed by explaining the pathway, not by repeating the screen.
options: Give him a second kit and only refer if that is also positive
Reassure him that a positive kit in a well man is usually a false alarm
Arrange a faecal occult blood test in the clinic instead of colonoscopy
Refer him for colonoscopy
Start him on a low-residue diet and repeat the kit in six months

D matches the rule on the facts given.

A positive bowel screening kit leads to colonoscopy. Repeating the kit can produce a false negative and delay diagnosis. Being asymptomatic does not change the pathway. The screening test is not confirmed by doing it again.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

items.question_text: A 32-year-old woman has postcoital bleeding for two months. Her last cervical screening test was 18 months ago and was negative for HPV. She asks for an early routine screening test because she is worried, and a friend has told her that a negative test last year means she can wait for the normal five-year interval. She is not pregnant. There is no cervical screening result that clears postcoital bleeding. Bleeding after sex is a symptom. It is assessed, not screened. A recent negative HPV test does not replace examination and appropriate referral. What is the most appropriate next step? She is inside the screening age range and her last test was negative, which is why the five-year interval would apply if she had no symptoms. She has a symptom. Postcoital bleeding needs clinical assessment of the cervix, not another screening sample to reassure her. An early routine test is the wrong pathway. The interval is for asymptomatic women. She is not asymptomatic. Examine and refer on the symptom, not on the calendar.
options: Assess the bleeding and refer. Do not treat this as a routine interval screen
Repeat the HPV test now and reassure her if it is negative
Tell her to wait until the five-year interval because the last test was negative
Start the oral contraceptive pill and review the bleeding in six months
Arrange a screening self-collection swab and discharge her
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Assess the bleeding and refer. Do not treat this as a routine interval screen

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
A symptom-free 58-year-old who is 26 months past a normal mammogram is due for BreastScreen mammography, not MRI or ultrasound prompted by density or an aunt's cancer.

2. THE RULE
Abnormal HPV result or postcoital bleeding is not a routine interval

3. WHY THIS OPTION
A matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Postcoital bleeding is a symptom. It is not managed by repeating a screening test or by waiting for the next interval. A recent negative HPV result does not clear the symptom. She needs assessment and referral, not a routine screen.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Assess the bleeding and refer. Do not treat this as a routine interval screen

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Invite a symptom-free woman aged 50–74 to BreastScreen every 2 years.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
BreastScreen invites women aged 50–74 for mammography every 2 years.

---

items.question_text: A 55-year-old man with no personal or family history of melanoma asks to be enrolled in a national skin-cancer screening program. He has read that Australia has the highest rate of melanoma and assumes there must be a mail-out or invitation program like BreastScreen. He has no changing moles and no symptom. A colleague says to enrol him in the national melanoma screen and arrange annual full-body photography on the program. There is no national population screening program for melanoma. High incidence is not the same as a screening program. What is the most appropriate advice? He is well and has no lesion of concern. Opportunistic skin checks in general practice are not a national screening program. There is no invitation, no mail-out, and no program to enrol him in. Advising sun protection and telling him to return if a mole changes is appropriate. Inventing a national melanoma screen is not. The same applies to average-risk ovarian screening and to routine PSA screening. High burden of disease does not create a program that does not exist.
options: Enrol him in the national melanoma screening program and arrange annual photography
Arrange a CA-125 and pelvic ultrasound as part of average-risk ovarian screening
Start annual PSA screening because there is a national prostate program
Reassure him that melanoma does not occur in Australia
Explain there is no national melanoma screening program to enrol him in
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Explain there is no national melanoma screening program to enrol him in

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
A symptom-free 58-year-old who is 26 months past a normal mammogram is due for BreastScreen mammography, not MRI or ultrasound prompted by density or an aunt's cancer.

2. THE RULE
No national PSA, melanoma or average-risk ovarian screening

3. WHY THIS OPTION
E matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Australia has no national population screening program for melanoma, average-risk ovarian cancer, or prostate cancer. A high incidence does not create a program. He should not be enrolled in a screen that does not exist. Sun protection and review of changing lesions is the advice, not a fictional program.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Explain there is no national melanoma screening program to enrol him in

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Invite a symptom-free woman aged 50–74 to BreastScreen every 2 years.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
BreastScreen invites women aged 50–74 for mammography every 2 years.

---

items.question_text: A term baby is born at 3 am in a Melbourne public hospital. The mother is hepatitis B surface-antigen negative, and the antenatal record is complete. Birth weight is 3400 g. The baby is well, breastfeeding, and has no risk factors for perinatal transmission. The night registrar is about to leave the ward and suggests leaving the birth dose of hepatitis B until the 6-week GP check, because the mother is negative and the baby looks well. The parents are happy to vaccinate and ask if delaying is safer. The midwife has the vaccine drawn up. There is no contraindication. Birth hepatitis B is given as soon as practicable, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 7 days, regardless of maternal status. Waiting for the 6-week check is the error. What is the most appropriate advice?  The antenatal serology is on the file and was repeated in the third trimester. There is no maternal risk behaviour that would change the plan. The baby has had vitamin K. The parents have no objection. Delaying to 6 weeks leaves a window the birth dose is designed to close. The dose should be given now, before the registrar leaves.  Observation for the usual post-vaccine period is planned. There is no family history of vaccine reaction. The 6-week check remains for the other infant vaccines. It is not a substitute for the birth dose of hepatitis B.  The parents ask if a negative mother means the baby cannot catch hepatitis B later. Explain that the birth dose is population protection, not only perinatal. Give it now.
options: Give the birth dose of hepatitis B now
Omit the birth dose because maternal surface antigen is negative
Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin instead of vaccine
Defer the dose until the 6-week check so it can be combined
Test the baby for surface antibody before any vaccine
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Give the birth dose of hepatitis B now

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
A well term baby of a surface-antigen-negative mother still receives the birth dose of hepatitis B now, not at 6 weeks.

2. THE RULE
Birth hepatitis B timing

3. WHY THIS OPTION
A matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Every infant is offered a birth dose of hepatitis B, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 7 days. Maternal surface-antigen negativity does not remove the birth dose. Immunoglobulin is added for babies of infectious mothers. It does not replace vaccine in this baby.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Give the birth dose of hepatitis B now

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Birth hepatitis B is given as soon as practicable, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 7 days.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
Birth hepatitis B is universal, ideally within 24 hours and by 7 days.

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

items.best_treatment: Give the birth dose of hepatitis B now

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin instead of vaccine Immunoglobulin is for babies of infectious mothers, with vaccine, not instead of it.

items.question_text: A 16-week-old infant in Adelaide is brought for vaccines that were missed after a move interstate. He is well, afebrile, and has had no intussusception. He has never had a rotavirus dose. The first dose of Rotarix cannot be started once the infant has turned 15 weeks. He is now 16 weeks. A locum suggests giving it anyway because the child is behind and the family are keen. The other infant vaccines that are due can still be given. Rotavirus is the one with the hard age limit on the first dose. Starting it now is outside the schedule. What is the most appropriate advice about rotavirus?  He is growing well and has no chronic gastrointestinal disease. The family moved at 10 weeks and missed the 4-month visit. Other due vaccines, including the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis and pneumococcal doses, can proceed. Only rotavirus has this upper age limit on the first dose. Explaining that clearly avoids a dose given outside the schedule.  The AIR confirms no rotavirus dose ever. He is past the 14-week and 6-day limit for the first Rotarix dose. Document the missed window so a later clinician does not try to start it. Continue the rest of the catch-up.  Write the age limit in the notes. The family are anxious about being behind. Reassure them the other vaccines proceed. Rotavirus does not.
options: Give the first rotavirus dose today and book the second in 8 weeks
Do not start rotavirus. The first Rotarix dose cannot be given once the infant has turned 15 weeks
Give rotavirus only if a stool viral PCR is negative
Replace rotavirus with an extra pneumococcal dose
Give both rotavirus doses today to finish the course
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Do not start rotavirus. The first Rotarix dose cannot be given once the infant has turned 15 weeks

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
At 16 weeks the first Rotarix dose is too late. Catch-up does not override that age limit.

2. THE RULE
Rotavirus age limit

3. WHY THIS OPTION
B matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
On the NIP the rotavirus product is Rotarix. The first dose must be given by 14 weeks, before the infant turns 15 weeks, and the second by 24 weeks. At 16 weeks he cannot start the course. The rest of the overdue infant schedule can still be planned. A negative stool test does not reopen the age window.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Do not start rotavirus. The first Rotarix dose cannot be given once the infant has turned 15 weeks

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
The first Rotarix dose cannot be started once the infant has turned 15 weeks.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
First Rotarix dose by 14 weeks, before turning 15 weeks. Second by 24 weeks.

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

items.best_treatment: Do not start rotavirus. The first Rotarix dose cannot be given once the infant has turned 15 weeks

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Give the first rotavirus dose today and book the second in 8 weeks The catch-up instinct is the trap. The upper age has already passed.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Give rotavirus only if a stool viral PCR is negative Viral clearance does not change the age limit.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Replace rotavirus with an extra pneumococcal dose Pneumococcal has its own schedule. It is not a substitute dose.

Other overdue infant vaccines are not cancelled by this rule.

items.question_text: A woman in Perth is 24 weeks pregnant in her second pregnancy. She received dTpa at 28 weeks in the last pregnancy, three years ago. She asks if she needs it again or if the previous dose covers this baby. She is well, with no contraindication to the vaccine. Pertussis vaccine is recommended at 20 to 32 weeks in each pregnancy, to protect the newborn. A dose in a previous pregnancy does not cover this one. She is inside the window now. What is the most appropriate advice?  She had no reaction to the previous dTpa. This pregnancy is uncomplicated. She is not near delivery. The point of the dose is transplacental antibody for the newborn, so it is repeated each pregnancy in the recommended window. A dose three years ago does not provide that for this baby. She should have it now.  Antibody from a dose years ago will have waned for the purpose of protecting this newborn. The recommendation is explicit: each pregnancy, 20 to 32 weeks. She is at 24 weeks. Give dTpa now.  She can have it in the antenatal clinic or at the GP. Either is fine. The error is skipping it because of a dose in the last pregnancy.
options: Skip dTpa because the last dose was within 10 years
Give dTpa only if a contact has pertussis
Give dTpa now, in this pregnancy
Defer dTpa until 37 weeks so the antibodies are fresher
Give a childhood DTPa formulation instead
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Give dTpa now, in this pregnancy

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
At 24 weeks she should have dTpa in this pregnancy. A dose 3 years ago does not protect this newborn.

2. THE RULE
Vaccines in pregnancy: pertussis, influenza, MMR, RSV

3. WHY THIS OPTION
C matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
A single dTpa dose is recommended in every pregnancy, preferably between 20 and 32 weeks, to protect the newborn. A dose 3 years ago does not cover this baby. Thirty-seven weeks is later than the preferred window.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Give dTpa now, in this pregnancy

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Pertussis vaccine is recommended at 20 to 32 weeks in each pregnancy.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
Pregnancy dTpa is once each pregnancy, preferably 20 to 32 weeks.

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Skip dTpa because the last dose was within 10 years The adult booster interval is not the pregnancy rule.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Give dTpa only if a contact has pertussis Pregnancy vaccination is routine, not outbreak-only.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Defer dTpa until 37 weeks so the antibodies are fresher The preferred window is 20 to 32 weeks.

The 10-year adult interval does not apply here.

items.question_text: A woman in Hobart is 8 weeks pregnant and asks for the influenza vaccine because her toddler is in childcare. A receptionist has told her to wait until the second trimester. She is well, with no egg anaphylaxis and no previous reaction to the vaccine. Influenza vaccine is inactivated and can be given at any stage of pregnancy, in every pregnancy. Waiting for the second trimester is unnecessary. What is the most appropriate advice?  She has no febrile illness today. The toddler's childcare has had several respiratory infections. Influenza in pregnancy protects her and the newborn. The inactivated vaccine has no trimester restriction. The receptionist's advice to wait is the old habit, not the current recommendation. She can be vaccinated today.  No live vaccine is being considered. Influenza is inactivated. First-trimester administration is acceptable and recommended when the vaccine is available. Do not defer to 13 weeks.  Childcare exposure is a reason to give it, not to delay. Any trimester is acceptable. Vaccinate today.  She has no contraindication. The toddler's childcare is the exposure that prompted the visit. That supports giving the vaccine, not delaying it. Any stage of pregnancy is acceptable for inactivated influenza vaccine.
options: Wait until 28 weeks, with the pertussis vaccine
Influenza vaccine is contraindicated before 12 weeks
Give live attenuated influenza vaccine today
Give inactivated influenza vaccine now
Test for influenza IgG and vaccinate only if negative
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Give inactivated influenza vaccine now

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
At 8 weeks she can have inactivated influenza vaccine now. It is not held until the third trimester.

2. THE RULE
Vaccines in pregnancy: pertussis, influenza, MMR, RSV

3. WHY THIS OPTION
D matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended at any stage of each pregnancy. Waiting for the third trimester leaves her uncovered through the first half of pregnancy. Live attenuated influenza vaccine is not the pregnancy product.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Give inactivated influenza vaccine now

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Influenza vaccine can be given at any stage of pregnancy, in every pregnancy.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended at any stage of every pregnancy.

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

items.best_treatment: Give inactivated influenza vaccine now

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Wait until 28 weeks, with the pertussis vaccine Pertussis has a preferred window. Influenza does not need to wait for it.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Influenza vaccine is contraindicated before 12 weeks There is no first-trimester ban on inactivated influenza vaccine.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Give live attenuated influenza vaccine today Live influenza vaccine is not used in pregnancy.

items.question_text: A woman in Cairns is 10 weeks pregnant. Her serology shows she is not immune to rubella. She is travelling to a region with a measles outbreak in six weeks and asks for MMR now so she is covered before she goes. MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy. It can be planned after delivery. Giving it now is the error. What is the most appropriate advice?  Rubella non-immunity is noted. MMR would address that, but not in pregnancy. Travel advice and post-exposure planning can be discussed. The vaccine itself waits until after delivery, when she is no longer pregnant. Giving a live vaccine now is contraindicated.  Postnatal MMR can be arranged before she leaves hospital or at the 6-week check, once pregnancy is over. Travel precautions are separate. The injection today is not MMR.  Document non-immunity and the plan for postnatal MMR. Do not give the live vaccine this trimester, whatever the travel date.  Travel in six weeks does not override the live-vaccine contraindication. Measles protection for a pregnant woman who is susceptible is a public-health and exposure question, not a reason to inject MMR today.
options: Give MMR today and repeat it after 4 weeks
Give MMR if a dating scan is normal
Give varicella vaccine instead, because it is safer in pregnancy
Delay travel advice and give MMR in the second trimester
Do not give MMR in pregnancy. Plan it after delivery
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Do not give MMR in pregnancy. Plan it after delivery

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
Non-immune rubella serology in a pregnant woman is a reason to plan MMR after delivery, not to give it now.

2. THE RULE
Vaccines in pregnancy: pertussis, influenza, MMR, RSV

3. WHY THIS OPTION
E matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy. Non-immune status and travel do not override that. Varicella vaccine is also live and also contraindicated. She can be vaccinated after delivery, and pregnancy should be avoided for 28 days after MMR.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Do not give MMR in pregnancy. Plan it after delivery

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
Live vaccines, including MMR and varicella, are contraindicated in pregnancy.

---

items.question_text: A 45-year-old man with a history of egg anaphylaxis, which required adrenaline, asks for the influenza vaccine. He is well today. A colleague says egg allergy is a contraindication and he should be referred to hospital for any dose. Egg anaphylaxis is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination in a setting that can treat anaphylaxis. He can be vaccinated here today. What is the most appropriate advice?  His egg anaphylaxis was five years ago and is well documented. He has no anaphylaxis to a previous influenza vaccine. The clinic has adrenaline and a place to observe him. Egg allergy, including anaphylaxis, is not a reason to withhold influenza vaccine in that setting. Hospital referral is not required for this indication.  Observe him for the recommended period after the dose. Adrenaline is available. That is the setting the advice assumes. Withholding the vaccine for egg anaphylaxis is outdated.  He has asked specifically about egg. The answer is that he can be vaccinated here. Do not send him away for that history.
options: Give inactivated influenza vaccine here today
Influenza vaccine is absolutely contraindicated after egg anaphylaxis
Skin-test him with raw egg white before any dose
Give the vaccine only after a graded egg challenge
Use half the dose and observe him at home
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Give inactivated influenza vaccine here today

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
Egg anaphylaxis does not stop inactivated influenza vaccine when the clinic can treat anaphylaxis.

2. THE RULE
True contraindication versus egg allergy and mild illness

3. WHY THIS OPTION
A matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Anaphylaxis to egg is not a contraindication to inactivated influenza vaccine. He can be vaccinated in a setting that can manage anaphylaxis. Skin testing and egg challenge are not the pathway, and a half dose is not a recommendation.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Give inactivated influenza vaccine here today

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Egg anaphylaxis is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination in a setting that can treat anaphylaxis.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
Egg allergy, including anaphylaxis, is not a flu-vaccine contraindication.

---

Record the anaphylaxis clearly so it is not repeated at the next visit. Other vaccines that he has tolerated can continue. This one stops. CORRECT ANSWER

B. Do not give this vaccine. Anaphylaxis after a previous dose is a contraindication

---

Anaphylaxis after a previous dose of a vaccine is a contraindication to that vaccine. A brand change, a half dose, or an antihistamine does not remove it. This is a medical contraindication, not a conscientious objection, and it should be confirmed and recorded by an approved practitioner.

items.question_text: A healthy child aged 8 months is having influenza vaccine for the first time. A parent asks if one dose is enough, as it is for older children. A healthy child aged 6 months to under 2 years needs two doses, at least 4 weeks apart, in the first year they are vaccinated. One dose is not enough this year. What is the most appropriate advice?  This is his first year of influenza vaccine. He is 8 months and healthy. Children from 6 months to under 2 years need two doses in that first year, at least four weeks apart. One dose, as for an older child, is not enough. Book the second.  First dose today, second in at least four weeks. Next year, if he is still under a relevant age, the schedule may be one dose. This first year is two.  Two doses this first season. Book the second before they leave. One dose is the older-child rule.  First influenza season, age 8 months, healthy. Two doses at least four weeks apart. One dose is insufficient this year.
options: One dose is enough because he is under 12 months
Influenza vaccine starts at 5 years
Give two doses, at least 4 weeks apart, this first year
Give a live intranasal vaccine because he is an infant
Serology between the two doses decides whether the second is needed
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Give two doses, at least 4 weeks apart, this first year

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
A healthy 7-month-old having influenza vaccine for the first time needs two doses at least 4 weeks apart.

2. THE RULE
Two influenza doses under 2 years

3. WHY THIS OPTION
C matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Healthy children aged 6 months to under 2 years need two doses in the first year they receive influenza vaccine, at least 4 weeks apart, then one dose in later years. A 7-month-old is inside that rule. The under-9 two-dose rule applies to children with a medical risk condition, not to every healthy child under 9. Serology does not sit between the two doses.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Give two doses, at least 4 weeks apart, this first year

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
A healthy child aged 6 months to under 2 years needs two influenza doses in the first year they are vaccinated.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR
First-year influenza vaccine in a healthy child aged 6 months to under 2 years is two doses.

---

items.question_text: An infant is due for meningococcal B vaccine. The parent has read that prophylactic paracetamol is no longer recommended with any vaccine and asks to skip it. Prophylactic paracetamol is recommended with meningococcal B vaccine in infants, to reduce fever. It should be given. What is the most appropriate advice?  Meningococcal B is associated with fever in infants. Prophylactic paracetamol is specifically recommended with it. The general advice against routine prophylactic paracetamol with other vaccines does not apply here. Give it as recommended.  Give the recommended doses of paracetamol around the meningococcal B injection. This is specific advice, not a general prophylactic habit. Do not skip it because of advice about other vaccines.  Paracetamol with infant MenB is recommended. Give the prophylactic doses. Do not omit them on general principles.  Infant MenB. Prophylactic paracetamol is recommended with this vaccine. General advice against routine prophylaxis does not apply. Give it.
options: Avoid all paracetamol for 48 hours after meningococcal B
Delay meningococcal B until 12 months to avoid fever
Give ibuprofen as the routine prophylactic medicine
Give prophylactic paracetamol with meningococcal B, as recommended
Skip meningococcal B if any fever risk is unacceptable
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Give prophylactic paracetamol with meningococcal B, as recommended

---

1. CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS
With infant meningococcal B, give the vaccine and give prophylactic paracetamol. Do not withhold paracetamol.

2. THE RULE
Paracetamol with infant MenB

3. WHY THIS OPTION
D matches the rule on the facts given.

4. THE TRAP
Prophylactic paracetamol is recommended for children under 2 years receiving meningococcal B vaccine. This is an exception to the usual advice not to give routine paracetamol at vaccination. Avoiding it because of a theoretical blunting concern is not the handbook advice. Delaying to 12 months, or skipping the dose, trades a common fever for a missed vaccine.

5. WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
The single fact that places this case on this rule, not a neighbouring one.

6. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE IT
Age, a relative's preference, a busy clinic, or a recent negative test does not create an exception.

7. THE NEXT STEP
Give prophylactic paracetamol with meningococcal B, as recommended

8. WHAT TO DOCUMENT
The assessment, the rule applied, and the action taken.

9. RELATED RULES
Prophylactic paracetamol is recommended with meningococcal B vaccine in infants.

10. MEMORY ANCHOR

---
